channel.title: The Discovery Wire
channel.description: Science, decoded — the experiments, the instruments, and the questions nobody has answered yet.

item.title: The Supernova Impostor: Chandra Finds What Keeps Making a Giant Star Erupt Every 113 Days
item.description: AT 2016blu in NGC 4559 has erupted at least 27 times since 2012 without destroying itself. NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory caught it mid-outburst in March 2026 — and found a hidden black hole or neutron star companion pulling material off it every 113 days.

item.title: Hera Just Saw the Side of Didymos DART Never Photographed
item.description: ESA's Hera spacecraft returned its first close-range image of the Didymos asteroid system on November 5, 2026 — a boulder-strewn face of Didymos that DART's camera never saw, with Dimorphos peeking from shadow.

item.title: A Lava World Circles Its Star Every 5.4 Hours — and Hubble Just Watched It Disappear Behind It
item.description: Hubble has detected the secondary eclipse of a rocky exoplanet for the first time. TOI-2431b is a 6.2-Earth-mass lava world with a 5.4-hour year and a dayside near 2,524 K — hot enough to melt rock.

item.title: Built to Chase the Universe's Biggest Explosions — Swift Came Home in Fire
item.description: NASA's Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory re-entered Earth's atmosphere on November 4, 2026, ending more than two decades of watching gamma-ray bursts. It made its last observation on October 20, a rescue mission failed in July, and the Sun itself hastened the end.

item.title: They Heard Hydrogen Clumping 4.5 Billion Years Ago — and the Cosmic Web Showed Up
item.description: The MeerKLASS collaboration has made the first measurement of large-scale cosmic hydrogen clustering with 21-cm intensity mapping — a decade of work, a signal 10,000 times fainter than the foreground noise, and a map of the universe drawn in hydrogen instead of light.

item.title: The Early Universe's Galaxies Were Too Bright. A Cosmic Leaf Blower May Explain Why.
item.description: JWST found more bright galaxies in the early universe than anyone expected. New simulations from the Flatiron Institute and UT Dallas suggest ultraviolet light from young star clusters acted like a leaf blower, clearing the fog of gas and dust so the starlight could reach us.

item.title: A Giant Planet Was Hiding in Two-Year-Old Webb Data — New Software Just Found It
item.description: Planets are a million times fainter than their stars, and Webb's own tiny wobbles bury them in glare. A Northwestern team's new method, FLIP, models the telescope itself — and pulled 51 Eridani b out of data where standard processing saw nothing.

item.title: When Should We Listen for Alien Signals? SETI Turns to Game Theory
item.description: A SETI Institute team is searching the anti-solar point — the one sky alignment two civilizations could independently pick without ever communicating — two to three nights a week for about four years. The pilot found no technosignature, but it was the first time anyone actually tested the idea.

item.title: To Deflect an Asteroid, Where You Aim Matters More Than Anyone Thought
item.description: New Sandia simulations show that an asteroid's lumpy, irregular shape can change the push from a nuclear X-ray burst by nearly fivefold depending on which side is hit — and change its spin by a factor of 17. Planetary defense, it turns out, is an aiming problem.

item.title: After 42 Years, Physicists Caught a Decay That Happens Once in 10 Billion
item.description: The upgraded LHCb experiment at CERN has found the first evidence for one of the rarest particle decays ever sought — a beauty particle transforming into two muons, a process predicted to occur only about once in every 10 billion beauty particles. At 3.2 sigma it is evidence, not yet a discovery — and a new window into the "Zeptoverse."

item.title: Neptune Was Hiding Its Trailing Trojans Behind the Milky Way
item.description: Astronomers have known Jupiter's Trojan asteroids since 1906, but Neptune's trailing cloud stayed elusive — crowded in front of the bright center of the Milky Way for a decade. Using early Rubin Observatory data, a Queen's University Belfast-led team has now identified two long-term stable trailing Trojans and a third candidate, doubling the known long-lived population.

item.title: It Looked Like One of the First Galaxies. Then It Moved.
item.description: A faint red object nicknamed Capotauro appeared to be a galaxy from about 100 million years after the Big Bang. Images 3.5 years apart show it shifted — it is actually a cold brown dwarf about 2,400 light-years away in our own Milky Way.

item.title: Earthquake Watch — The Week's Biggest Quake Nobody Felt, and a Tiny One 522 People Did
item.description: In the seven days ending November 3, the USGS catalog logged 349 earthquakes of magnitude 2.5 or greater — five of them magnitude 6 or stronger, all Green alert. The most-reported quake of the week was a magnitude 2.7 in California.

item.title: The Case of the Missing Oxygen: Hubble Finds Dwarf Galaxies Keep Only a Tenth of What Their Stars Make
item.description: A Hubble census of 37 nearby dwarf galaxies found they retain just 4% to 25% of the oxygen their stars produced — about 11% on average. Supernova-driven winds are carrying the rest away, more effectively than models predicted.

item.title: Earthquake Watch — A Quiet Day That Still Logged 204 Quakes
item.description: In the 24 hours ending this morning, the USGS catalog recorded 20 earthquakes of magnitude 4.5 or stronger — and not one above 5.1. Then a 5.3 south of Crete reminded everyone the day was not over.

item.title: Mars Dust Is Kinder to Spacesuits Than Moon Dust — and Sneakier
item.description: Perseverance has spent 1,645 Martian days wearing tiny swatches of spacesuit fabric. The good news: Mars dust is smooth and barely wears the material. The catch: some of it is 100 nanometers wide and laced with toxic perchlorates.

item.title: In 17 Days, Light Itself Will Need a Full Day to Reach Our Farthest Machine
item.description: On November 18, 2026, NASA's Voyager 1 — launched in 1977 — will cross the one-light-day mark, 16.1 billion miles from the Sun. A signal sent that morning will not arrive until the next day.

item.title: A World Maybe 1,000 Kilometers Wide Was Hiding Beyond Pluto
item.description: The Vera C. Rubin Observatory has found its first dwarf planet candidate, 2026 ED138 — a large, bright, red world beyond Neptune that sat unnoticed in survey data and in archives going back to 2016.

item.title: Something Is Watching From 7,500 Light-Years Away — Webb and Hubble Catch the Cat's Head Nebula Staring Back
item.description: Released just before Halloween, NASA's new Webb and Hubble views of the Cat's Head Nebula show a dusty pillar inside the Carina Nebula being carved by massive stars — with a newborn star for an eye.

item.title: Earthquake Watch — Five M5+ Quakes in Under Three Hours off Vanuatu
item.description: A magnitude 6.0 struck northwest of Port-Olry, Vanuatu on October 28 — the middle of a tight cluster of five magnitude 5.0-or-greater events in about two hours and 52 minutes, all shallow, all offshore, Green alert.
